Finnish women voted nationally in 1906. Swiss women had to wait until 1971, 65 years later. Here's when women could first vote in each European country.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Finland went first. In 1906, while still an autonomous Grand Duchy inside the Russian Empire, it gave women the vote. At the 1907 election, 19 women won seats, the first female MPs anywhere in the world.

2/ Norway came next in 1913, when its parliament voted unanimously for universal women's suffrage. It's often called the first independent country in Europe to do it. Iceland and Denmark followed in 1915.

3/ Then the big wave around WWI: Russia 1917, Germany, Poland, Austria and the UK 1918, Sweden and the Netherlands 1919. In Britain, though, women had to be over 30 and meet property rules until equal voting came in 1928.

4/ France, home of the Rights of Man, extended the vote to women only by an ordinance of April 1944. Women first voted in the municipal elections of April 1945. Italy decreed women's suffrage in 1945 as well.
5/ Greece let some women vote in local elections from 1930, under narrow rules. Full national voting rights and the right to run for office only arrived on 28 May 1952.

6/ Switzerland: in 1959 Swiss men rejected women's suffrage by about two to one. The federal vote finally passed in February 1971, and the half-canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden held out until a federal court forced it in 1990.
Monaco (1962), Andorra (1970) and Liechtenstein (1984) came even later. France 1944 or Switzerland 1971: which date surprises you more? Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
